title: Episode 31: Diamondfield Jack and the Cassia County Sheep War
description:
In the 1890s, southern Idaho was torn by a vicious range war between powerful cattle syndicates and sheep herders. The Sparks-Harrell cattle company hired a boastful young gunslinger named 'Diamondfield Jack' Davis to patrol the range. Wrongfully convicted of murdering two sheepherders, Jack survived three stays of execution—once within three hours of the noose—before being fully pardoned when the real killers confessed, going on to strike gold in Nevada.

FULL TRANSCRIPT:

[Rebecca - Host]
Welcome to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. In the late nineteenth century, the American West was gripped by an undeclared civil war: the bitter, bloody range war between cattlemen and sheep ranchers. Cattlemen claimed that sheep tore up the grass by the roots and left a foul scent that caused cows to starve. In southern Idaho's Cassia County, that hatred boiled over into murder. In eighteen ninety-six, two young sheepmen were shot dead in their camp. Suspicion immediately fell upon a flamboyant, fast-talking young gunslinger named Diamondfield Jack Davis, hired by a massive cattle company to terrorize sheepherders. What followed was one of the most bizarre legal sagas in frontier history: a man sentenced to hang three separate times, escaping the gallows at the final second, who lived to strike a multi-million-dollar fortune in gold. Here is George with the story.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT I: THE CATTLE KING AND THE SHEEP DEADLINES
In the eighteen nineties, the sagebrush plains and river canyons of Cassia County, Idaho were the scene of an escalating, violent range war. On one side stood the mighty Sparks-Harrell Cattle Company, a colossal corporate livestock syndicate co-owned by Nevada cattle baron and future governor John Sparks. Sparks-Harrell grazed more than one hundred and fifty thousand head of cattle across three million acres of open public rangeland stretching from northern Nevada's Elko County straight into the Snake River Valley of southern Idaho. On the other side were dozens of independent Mormon and Basque sheep herders, who brought tens of thousands of sheep onto the public lands under the protection of federal homestead laws. Cattlemen were furious, maintaining that sheep cropped the fragile desert bunchgrass so close to the soil that cattle starved, and claiming that cows possessed an instinctive aversion to the scent left by sheep hooves. The cattle barons established arbitrary 'deadlines'—imaginary boundaries drawn across the sagebrush valleys—warning sheepmen that if a single band of sheep crossed the line, both the animals and their herders would be exterminated. To enforce these deadlines, cattle companies formed private armies of armed cowboys who waged a merciless campaign of terror: poisoning sheep salt licks with strychnine, clubbing entire flocks to death in midnight raids, and firing volleys of rifle fire into the canvas sheep wagons of sleeping herders. As the summer heat intensified, tempers frayed across the sagebrush plains. Armed bands of cattle riders guarded mountain passes and springs, declaring that sheep herders who dared cross the invisible boundary would face swift, extrajudicial retribution.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT II: ENTER DIAMONDFIELD JACK
Into this tense powder keg stepped one of the most colorful characters in the annals of Western gunfighters: Jackson Lee Davis, universally known as 'Diamondfield Jack.' Born in Virginia, Jack was a slight, swaggering youth in his mid-twenties with a glib tongue, sharp blue eyes, and an insatiable desire for frontier notoriety. He earned his colorful moniker after claiming to have discovered fabulously rich diamond deposits in the Idaho desert, though not a single diamond was ever found. In eighteen ninety-five, the Sparks-Harrell cattle syndicate hired Diamondfield Jack as a 'range detective' at the princely wage of one hundred and fifty dollars a month—nearly five times what an ordinary cowboy earned. Jack's primary job was simple: ride the perimeter deadlines armed with a pair of silver-plated Colt revolvers and a Winchester rifle, shooting sheep that strayed across the line and bragging in every saloon from Shoshone to Elko that he was paid to put holes in sheepherders. Jack was a flamboyant braggart who loved dramatic grandstanding, but despite his violent talk, he was widely regarded by those who knew him as far more theatrical than lethal. Local newspapers described Jack as a walking arsenal, noting his twin revolvers with mother-of-pearl grips and his habit of wearing two cartridge belts crisscrossed over his chest in the Mexican bandolier style.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT III: DOUBLE MURDER AT DEEP CREEK
The comedic posturing turned to deadly tragedy on the freezing morning of February fourth, eighteen ninety-six. At a remote sheepherder camp near Deep Creek in Cassia County, two young Mormon sheepherders named John Wilson and Daniel Cummings were discovered dead inside their canvas sheep wagon. Both men had been shot multiple times through the head with forty-five caliber bullets while preparing their morning breakfast. Their sheep dogs were found whining beside their bodies, and their band of sheep was wandering aimlessly across the sagebrush. The murders sent shockwaves of fury through the local Mormon communities of southern Idaho. Feeling oppressed by the out-of-state Nevada cattle barons, the local population demanded blood. Because Diamondfield Jack had spent the previous six months publicly boasting in every barroom that he would shoot any sheepman who crossed the deadline, suspicion immediately and exclusively centered upon him. Detectives discovered forty-five caliber cartridges near the wagon, the same caliber as Jack's pistols. Jack had been miles away at a Nevada ranch at the time of the murders, but recognizing that an angry lynch mob was forming, he fled south into Arizona. The chilling discovery of the two young herders sent waves of dread through every isolated homestead in the county. Families barricaded their cabin doors at night, fearing that a ruthless gang of cattle assassins was systematically purging the territory.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT IV: THE TRIAL OF THE CENTURY IN ALBION
Jack was captured in Yuma, Arizona, in eighteen ninety-seven and brought back in heavy leg irons to Albion, the rugged county seat of Cassia County. His trial became a legendary frontier courtroom showdown that captivated the entire Pacific Northwest. The tiny wooden courthouse was packed with armed partisans; cattlemen sat on one side in leather chaps with revolvers in their holsters, while Mormon sheepmen glared across the aisle in somber black suits. The prosecution was led by an ambitious, fiery young attorney named William E. Borah—later to become one of the most powerful and celebrated United States Senators in American history, known as the 'Lion of Idaho.' Borah delivered soaring, theatrical orations, portraying Jack as a ruthless corporate hitman who murdered innocent homesteaders in cold blood for cattle baron gold. In defense of their employee, the Sparks-Harrell syndicate spared no expense, retaining Jack's defense counsel: James H. Hawley, Idaho's premier criminal defense lawyer and future governor of the state. Despite Hawley presenting unimpeachable alibi witnesses proving that Jack was eating breakfast at a Nevada ranch seventy miles away across the border on the morning of the killings, the all-Mormon jury was determined to strike a blow against the cattle syndicate. After brief deliberations, the jury found Diamondfield Jack guilty of first-degree murder, and the judge sentenced him to hang by the neck until dead on June fourth, eighteen ninety-seven. The atmosphere inside the Albion courtroom was electric with tension. Outside on the dirt square, armed cowboys and grim-faced Mormon farmers stood in separate clusters, fingers resting nervously on the triggers of their holstered weapons.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT V: THE SCAFFOLD AND THE REAL KILLERS CONFESS
What followed was an extraordinary legal rollercoaster that spanned nearly six years. Hawley filed appeal after appeal, winning temporary reprieves just days before scheduled executions. In eighteen ninety-nine, the gallows was erected on the courthouse lawn in Albion, and Jack was measured for his coffin; three hours before the trap was set to drop, a stay of execution arrived from the state supreme court. Then, in nineteen hundred, two prominent Sparks-Harrell cattlemen named James Bower and Jeff Gray walked into an attorney's office and signed formal confessions: they had killed Wilson and Cummings in a spontaneous, self-defense shootout at the sheep wagon after the sheepherders fired on them. Jack was completely innocent and had not been present at the scene. Yet, astoundingly, the state of Idaho refused to release Jack! The two cattlemen were tried for murder in a different county and acquitted on grounds of self-defense. However, because legal technicalities prevented newly discovered evidence from overturning a settled verdict, Jack remained locked in death row, sentenced to hang for a murder that two other men had legally admitted committing. Outraged by the absurdity, attorney Hawley and even his prosecutor William Borah joined forces to lobby the State Board of Pardons. Finally, in December nineteen oh-two, Governor Frank Hunt signed an unconditional executive pardon, and Diamondfield Jack walked out of prison a free man. When Jack finally walked out of the prison gates into the crisp Boise air, he was met by a cheering crowd of admirers who had come to view the young gunfighter as an immortal symbol of resilience against institutional corruption.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VI: FROM DEATH ROW TO GOLD MILLIONAIRE
Jack left Idaho behind and rode directly south to Nevada, where the great gold boom of Tonopah and Goldfield was erupting. Partnering with a savvy prospector, Jack grubstaked a gold claim in the desert south of Goldfield. Miraculously, the claim turned out to be fabulously wealthy, and Jack named the camp 'Diamondfield'—finally making his eccentric nickname a reality. Jack sold his mining properties for over a quarter of a million dollars, purchased fleets of luxury automobiles, wore diamond stickpins and tailored silk suits, and lived like a king in the finest hotels of Reno and San Francisco. He participated in Nevada politics, survived several more shootouts, and loved recounting the story of how he was sentenced to hang three times for a crime he never committed. He was a regular fixture in the high-stakes gaming rooms of Tonopah, where he frequently bought champagne for entire saloons, toasting the memory of the Idaho hangman who had never managed to drop the trap beneath his boots.

[George - Storyteller]
ACT VII: THE FREMONT STREET TAXI AND THE LEGEND
Diamondfield Jack's extraordinary life of narrow escapes and frontier drama finally concluded in January nineteen thirty-four in Las Vegas, Nevada. Ironically, the man who had faced down armed posses, lynching mobs, rival gunfighters, and three dates with the hangman's scaffold was not felled by lead or hemp. At the age of sixty-four, while walking across Fremont Street near downtown Las Vegas, Jack was struck by a speeding taxicab. He succumbed to his injuries in the hospital shortly afterward, carrying his colorful memories into the great beyond. His life remains an indelible chronicle of the transition of the American West: beginning in the violent, lawless cattle range wars of the late nineteenth century and concluding in the neon glare of twentieth-century Nevada. Diamondfield Jack Davis stands as one of the most improbable and legendary figures of frontier lore—a swaggering braggart whose courtroom survival proved that in the American West, truth is always far stranger and more thrilling than any dime-novel fiction.

[Rebecca - Host]
CONCLUSION
Diamondfield Jack's miraculous escape from the gallows is a legendary testament to frontier drama, legal irony, and the chaotic clash between cattle and sheep that shaped the American West. Thank you for listening to Most Fascinating Stories. I'm Rebecca. Join us next Tuesday as we head to Montana for the brutal corporate war between the Copper Kings. Until then, stay curious.
